title: 20 Ways to Advertise Your Event for Free
summary: Advertise your event for free using 20 real tactics for social media, email, and local partnerships. See how InEvent supports the rest of your planning.
body_markdown:
[Marketing](https://inevent.com/blog/marketing)


###### Posted on September 18, 2026


Planning an event takes a lot of work. Getting people to actually show up takes even more. Good news: you don’t need a big ad budget to


**advertise your event for free** . You need the right channels and a plan for using them; that’s it. This guide walks through 20 real, no-cost ways to get the word out. They’re grouped by where you’ll actually use them: social media, free listings, what you already have, other people’s audiences, and your event itself.

##


**Free Ways to Advertise Your Event on Social Media**


### **1. Build an Event Page and a Simple Hashtag**


Create one official event page on Facebook or Instagram, then pick a short hashtag people can actually remember. Use it every time you post, and have your team do the same. Nothing kills a hashtag search faster than three different spellings of your event name floating around.


### **2. Post Countdown Teasers and Behind-the-Scenes Clips**


A short clip of a speaker rehearsing, a room getting set up, or swag being packed does more for excitement than another announcement graphic ever will. Post these for weeks, not just the day before.


[Statista’s tracking of social platforms used by marketers](https://www.statista.com/statistics/259390/social-media-platforms-used-by-marketers-worldwide/) still puts Facebook at the top for organic reach, so it’s not a bad place to kick off your countdown.


### **3. Run a Simple Giveaway**


Offer one free ticket, a front-row seat, or a small prize to anyone who shares your event post or tags a friend who might want to come. Keep the entry rules short. Three steps to enter means three chances for people to give up halfway through.


### **4. Join Real Conversations in Relevant Facebook and LinkedIn Groups**


Find the groups where your target attendees already hang out. Industry groups, local business groups, alumni groups, that kind of thing. Answer questions and add value before you mention your event at all. Once you’ve shown up a few times, a mention reads like a helpful tip, not a cold pitch.


### **5. Ask Speakers and Attendees to Share Their Own Countdown Posts**


People trust posts from other people more than posts from a brand account. Send your speakers and a few early registrants a ready-made graphic and a couple of lines they can copy, then ask them to post it in their own words. A personal post from a speaker usually reaches people your own account never will.


##


**Where Can You Advertise Your Event for Free?**


The best places for free event advertising are the ones your exact audience already checks, like local event calendars, industry-specific listing sites, and business directories. These free event posting sites get less competition than big general platforms, and most let you post events for free with no listing fee at all.


Still narrowing down where to advertise events for free? Start with your industry before your city, then check where to post events for free more broadly once those closer options are covered.


### **6. List Your Event on Free Community and Industry Calendars**


A few worth checking for almost any event:


- Your local Chamber of Commerce’s event calendar


- 10Times, for industry conferences and trade events


- Evvnt, which syndicates listings across hundreds of regional sites and local publications at once


- Meetup groups related to your topic or industry


- Google Business Profile’s built-in “Add an event” feature


- Newsletters or calendars run by professional associations in your field


Any one of these is a legitimate way to advertise events for free without spending a cent on placement.


##


**Free Ways to Use What You Already Have**


### **7. Email Your Existing List**


If you have any kind of email list, whether that’s customers, newsletter subscribers, or past attendees, it’s usually your highest-converting free channel. Send a first announcement, then two or three reminders spaced out over the following weeks.


**[MarketingProfs’ research on event marketing channels](https://www.marketingprofs.com/charts/2012/7219/social-media-effective-tool-for-event-marketers)** has long found that email beats social media for turning interest into actual registrations, even when social gets all the attention.


### **8. Turn Your Website Into an Event Hub**


Add one dedicated page for your event: the date, location, speakers, and a clear registration button. Link to it from your homepage banner and your blog. Wherever someone lands on your site, they should be able to find your event in one click.


### **9. Re-Invite People Who Came Last Time**


Past attendees already know your event is worth their time. Pull your list from last time and send a personal-feeling invite, ideally with an early-bird perk for being a returning face.


### **10. Add Your Event to Your Email Signature**


Every email your team sends is a free ad slot you’re not using. Add a one-line mention of your event and a link to your signature for a few weeks before the date. It costs nothing and reaches everyone your team already emails.


### **11. Turn Your Event’s Topic Into Content People Find on Their Own**


Write a short blog post, record a quick video, or answer a question your event covers, and publish it before the event. Link back to your registration page at the end. People searching for that topic will find your content first, and your event becomes the natural next step instead of a cold pitch.


##


**Free Ways to Borrow Other People’s Audiences**


### **12. Partner With Nearby Businesses or Organizations**


Ask a nearby coffee shop, coworking space, or community group to display your flyer, or mention your event to their list. Offer to do the same for one of theirs. Works best when your audiences overlap but you’re not stepping on each other’s toes. It’s a simple, mutual way to advertise events for free that costs neither side anything but goodwill.


### **13. Ask Speakers and Sponsors to Post to Their Own Networks**


Give your speakers and sponsors a simple one-page kit: a few sentences about the event, a graphic, and the registration link. Most are happy to share it with their own following. It makes them look good too.


### **14. Pitch Yourself as a Guest on a Relevant Podcast**


Find one or two podcasts your target attendees already listen to, and pitch yourself or a speaker as a guest. A 20-minute conversation about your event’s topic reaches a warm, already-interested audience in a way no banner ad ever could.


### **15. Reach Out to Alumni Groups or Professional Associations**


If your event connects to a school, certification body, or professional association, ask if they’ll mention it in their newsletter or member group. These groups want to share relevant events with their members. It costs you nothing but the ask.


### **16. Write a One-Page Case for Why Someone Should Attend**


Some of your best potential attendees need to convince a manager or a committee before they can even say yes. Write a short, one-page summary of what your event covers and why it’s worth the time, then make it easy to download and forward. ##


**Free Ways to Turn Your Event Itself Into Promotion**


Some of the best free promotion doesn’t come from marketing at all. It comes from how smooth the event feels to actually attend. InEvent is built by a fully remote team spread across 13+ countries, and its registration, check-in, and streaming tools are designed with exactly this in mind. Fewer friction points, more people talking about your event afterward.


### **17. Make Registration So Easy People Actually Finish It**


A registration form with too many fields loses people before they ever hit submit, and a lost registrant can’t share your event with anyone. Keep the form short. Make sure it works on a phone. See how


[InEvent’s registration and RSVP tools](https://inevent.com/en/registration-forms-rsvp-invites.php) handle this if you want a smoother starting point.


### **18. Make Check-In Fast Enough That People Post About It**


A long check-in line is one of the first things people complain about online. A fast one is one of the first things they praise. InEvent’s event strategists point out that a quick, well-organized check-in sets the tone for the whole event before a single session starts. Tools like


[InEvent’s badge printing and check-in](https://inevent.com/en/pass-event-quick-checkin.php) are built to keep that line moving.


### **19. Let People Preview the Event With a Short Livestream Clip**


Stream a few minutes of a keynote, a panel, or even the room filling up, then clip it for social media afterward. This works well for hybrid or


[virtual and hybrid events](https://inevent.com/en/go-beyond-virtual-hybrid-vh-events.php) , since a short preview gives people who couldn’t attend a reason to register for the next one. Check out our


**[hybrid event ideas](https://inevent.com/blog/events/hybrid-event-ideas.html)** for more ways to make a hybrid format work in your favor.


### **20. Get Attendees Talking to Each Other Before the Event Even Starts**


Attendees who start networking before the event are more likely to post about it, invite a colleague, or show up already excited instead of lukewarm. InEvent’s networking and AI matchmaking tools introduce attendees to relevant people before the event begins. Registration becomes the start of the buzz, not the end.


**Team Tip:** InEvent event strategists recommend sending your very first save-the-date note before your registration page is even finished. Early interest tells you whether your event idea is landing. You can always follow up with a polished page once it’s built.


##


**How Early Should You Start Advertising Your Event for Free?**


Most free channels need four to six weeks to build real momentum, since word of mouth and organic posts take time to spread. For bigger events, start eight weeks out with the channels you own: email and your website. Then layer in social media and partnerships as the date gets closer, saving your final push for the last week or two.


##


**Frequently Asked Questions**


### **How do I advertise an event for free?**


Start with what you already control: your email list, your website, and your social accounts. Layer in free event listing sites, partnerships with nearby businesses, and ask speakers or sponsors to share with their own networks. A few free channels working together beats relying on just one.


### **Where can I promote my event for free?**


Local Chamber of Commerce calendars, 10Times, Evvnt, Meetup groups, Google Business Profile, and industry association newsletters all count as free event posting sites. Facebook, Instagram, and LinkedIn work too, as long as you’re posting instead of paying to boost.


### **How do I promote a free event?**


The same way you’d promote a paid one: clear messaging, an easy registration process, and consistent posting in the weeks leading up to it. A free ticket removes one barrier. People still need a reason and a reminder to show up.


### **What’s the single best free way to advertise an event?**


Email your existing list first. It’s usually the highest-converting free channel, because you’re reaching people who already know and trust you instead of a cold audience on social media.


##


Advertise Your Event for Free, Starting Today


When you set out to advertise your event for free, you don’t need a paid ad budget to get people through the door. Start with the channels you already own. Add a few free listings and local partnerships. Then give people something worth sharing once they actually show up.
